passage: Come, sit, Meera beta. You asked how to help a friend without disappearing yourself, so listen to Pooja's story. I was twenty. My friend Vasudha called me at two, at four, in the middle of lectures. I felt so important, beta, the only one she trusted. And so tired that I fell asleep on the bus. My mother said, "You are not her doctor." I was angry with Ma for a week. Then one night I said, "Vasudha, I love you, but I can't be your only support. Let's meet the college counsellor together, and call your sister too." She cried. I cried. I sat with her at the first appointment, but I stopped picking up every single call. It felt like betrayal then. It was also the first time she got real help.

qa.q: How old was Pooja when Vasudha started calling at all hours?
How did Pooja feel about being Vasudha's only support?
qa.a: Important and needed, yet so tired that Pooja fell asleep on the bus.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that joined care with limits?
qa.a: Pooja suggested going to the college counsellor together, urged Vasudha to call her sister, and stopped picking up every single call.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt when Pooja stopped answering every call?
qa.a: She may have feared being dropped, and she cried, but the change also led her to real help at the appointment.

grounding: An elder recalls a friend who relied on her for everything: needed and drained, she set limits and steered the friend toward professional help.
